content: Hepatitis D virus (HDV) RNA levels in individuals with HDV infection can vary over time. This variability should be taken into account in clinical practice, and repeat testing may be necessary to confirm ongoing active infection or potential clearance of HDV RNA. Monitoring and Evaluation Systems It is essential to monitor and evaluate HDV testing approaches, including universal and risk-based testing strategies, as well as laboratory-based reflex testing. Regular reporting to healthcare providers and laboratory managers can help improve the quality of care. A database of individuals with HDV can be created using clinical or laboratory records and integrated into national hepatitis B virus (HBV) reporting systems to track testing, diagnosis, and treatment indicators. Research Gaps in HDV Testing High-quality data are critical to guide future HDV testing strategies and recommendations. There is a lack of data on HDV infection in children, adolescents, and pregnant women. Cost-effectiveness modeling and feasibility studies for universal HDV testing in lowand middle-income countries with varying epidemiological scenarios are needed, particularly in regions with high HBV prevalence but low HDV prevalence. The diagnostic performance of HDV serological assays and nucleic acid tests (NATs) requires validation, including the development of international reference standards for key genotypes. Priority should also be given to developing rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for anti-HDV to facilitate decentralized testing and care, especially in resource-limited settings. Fully automated NATs capable of accurate and reliable quantitative HDV RNA detection across all genotypes should be developed. Additionally, the impact, cost-effectiveness, and feasibility of anti-HDV reflex testing on care uptake and linkage in different settings need to be assessed. HBV Service Delivery and Monitoring The 2022 global health sector strategies aim to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health problem by 2030. However, as of 2019, only 10% of the estimated 296 million people with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) globally had been diagnosed, and only 2% were receiving treatment. Achieving the elimination goals will require significant scaling up of testing and case-finding, as well as simplifying and decentralizing service delivery to improve access and adherence to long-term antiviral therapy. Historically, hepatitis B and C testing and treatment have relied on specialist-led care in hospital settings. Even when testing occurred at the community level, referral to hospital-based care often resulted in significant patient attrition. Decentralizing HIV treatment services to peripheral health facilities and community-based venues has been a key factor in the successful global scale-up of antiretroviral therapy (ART), improving testing and treatment uptake while reducing loss to follow-up. Similarly, the availability of short-course, curative, pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral regimens for hepatitis C has enabled greater decentralization of care. The 2018 and 2022 WHO guidelines on hepatitis C emphasized simplified service delivery, including decentralization, integration of hepatitis testing and care with existing services, and task-sharing with non-specialist healthcare workers. While direct evidence for hepatitis B service delivery remains limited, similar principles can be applied to CHB care. This includes strategies to promote long-term adherence and retention in care, as most individuals with CHB require lifelong antiviral therapy. Strategies to Improve CHB Care 1. Promoting Testing and Linkage to Care: Strategies include using dried blood spots for serological and virological testing, peer and lay health worker support in community settings, electronic reminders for facility-based testing, and integrating testing into other health services. 2. Supporting Long-Term Adherence to Antiviral Therapy: Effective interventions include peer counseling, mobile phone text reminders, cognitive behavioral therapy, behavioral skills training, and medication adherence training. 3. Enhancing Retention in Care: Strategies include lay adherence counselors, peer and family support, and adherence clubs. Tracing and re-engaging individuals who have disengaged from care is also critical. 4. Integrating Hepatitis Services with Other Health Services: This includes providing hepatitis testing in antenatal clinics, ART clinics, and TB clinics, as well as integrating hepatitis B diagnosis with existing diagnostic platforms and laboratory services. 5. Decentralizing Testing and Treatment: Expanding services to primary health facilities or HIV/ART clinics can improve access to care. Task-sharing and differentiated care approaches are key to facilitating this. 6. Task-Sharing: Training and mentoring healthcare workers and peer workers can support task-sharing to improve service delivery. 7. Differentiated Care Strategies: Assessing individual care needs and referring complex cases to specialists as appropriate can optimize care delivery. 8. Community Engagement and Peer Support: Addressing stigma and discrimination through community engagement can improve access to services and linkage to care. Evidence from HIV and HCV Care Decentralized and integrated care models for HIV and HCV have demonstrated improved testing and treatment uptake, as well as better retention in care. For example, community-based HIV testing and treatment at lower-level health facilities have been shown to increase ART uptake and viral load suppression. Peer counseling, text messaging, and cognitive behavioral therapy have been effective in improving ART adherence. Community-based interventions, such as adherence clubs and patient advocates, have also been successful in retaining individuals in care. Integration of Hepatitis Testing and Care Integrating hepatitis B testing and care with other health services can improve access and efficiency. For example, testing for CHB can be offered in antenatal clinics, ART clinics, and TB clinics. Multi-disease diagnostic platforms can facilitate integrated testing for HIV, HBV, and HCV using a single specimen, improving efficiency and reducing costs. Shared use of multi-disease testing devices for HBV DNA testing can further enhance access and system efficiency. In summary, achieving the elimination of viral hepatitis as a public health problem will require a combination of strategies, including decentralization, integration, task-sharing, and community engagement, to improve access to testing, treatment, and long-term care.
